newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finn study sees risk of EU break-up over legitimacy.
newsitem.headline: Finn study sees risk of EU break-up over legitimacy.

text.p: The European Union could disintegrate due to legitimacy problems linked to European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the planned European central bank (ECB), a study by a Finnish think-tank said on Wednesday.

"From the legitimacy point of view, the European single market project, to be completed with the single currency and central bank, is an inherently contradictory one," senior researcher Heikki Patomaki at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs wrote in a new book "The Politics of Economic and Monetary Union".
The third phase of EMU amounts to a transfer of authority from national bodies to European bodies justified by "the alleged benefits of the single market," he said.
Legitimacy problems caused by the implementation of necessary reforms for EMU in the longer run could lead to disintegration of the EU, said Patomaki.
"The convergence criteria, the aim of economic stability, and the priority given to the fight against inflation are widely perceived to be co-causing unemployment," Patomaki said.

Another reason for opposition to EMU was the view of the single currency as a federalist project. Even 40 years after the treaty of Rome there is a lack of solidarity between the people of the EU, he said.
Patomaki also pointed out that the quest to justify what cannot be justified may actually lead to a wider legitimacy crisis.
Through its move towards an independent and unaccountable central bank the EU was undermining the conditions for finding new sources of legitimisation for itself, Patomaki said.

In another of the book's seven articles, Teivo Teivainen, lecturer at the Helsinki University, wrote that in the field of monetary policy, Europe's democratic institutions would be left with "basically decorative functions".
The creation of a European Central Bank would transfer governance to "unelected and non-accountable bodies," he said.
Stephen Gill, political sciences professor at York University in Toronto, Canada, also agreed in the book that EMU "eats away at processes of political accountability and democracy."

The obsession with zero inflation reflected the interests of institutional investors, banks and multinational firms, who Gill claimed had to a large extent influenced the substance of the Maastricht Treaty. --Helsinki newsroom +358-9-680 50 245, e-mail news@reuters.fi
